hints: Focus on the word only in the question. Tumour cells still divide by normal mitosis, so ask yourself which stages they still must go through.
Think about what makes division uncontrolled and rapid. Which part of the cell cycle normally takes the longest time, and what happens if checkpoints in that part are skipped?
walkthrough:
**Remember what a tumour cell is doing**

Tumour cells are dividing by mitosis over and over again, without stopping. That means they still need all the normal stages of mitosis and cytokinesis to make two cells.

So they do not skip metaphase or cytokinesis, they just do the whole cycle more often.

**Think about where time is saved**

In a normal cell cycle, interphase (G1 + S + G2) is by far the longest part. It is when the cell grows, copies DNA and is checked at checkpoints.

In tumour cells, control genes are faulty, so checkpoints are ignored and interphase is rushed through. The total cell cycle gets much shorter.

**Use the word only to decide**

We need something true for tumour cells but not for normal dividing cells. Normal cells also go through metaphase and cytokinesis, and normal body cells can also carry mutated DNA without forming a tumour.

Only the shortened interphase and rapid cycling is characteristic of the uncontrolled tumour cells here, so C is the best answer.

options.A: False. Tumour cells still carry out full mitosis, including metaphase when chromosomes line up on the equator.
options.B: False. Tumour cells still divide their cytoplasm by cytokinesis to form two separate daughter cells.
options.C: Correct. Tumour cells skip normal interphase checkpoints and controls, so G1 and G2 are much shorter and the cells divide again very quickly.
options.D: False. Many normal cells contain mutated DNA that is repaired or has no effect, so this is not unique to tumour cells only.
